title: Manhattan
summary: Manhattan is included among Long Island and adjacent island Native place names. Because Manhattan sits in Lenape/Munsee language territory, the name should not be flattened into a generic Algonquian label. The blue marker orients readers to the modern island, not an exact historic site.
map_geometry_source: Approximate modern central Manhattan Island coordinate used for a general adjacent-island placename marker.
why_this_matters: Manhattan preserves an Indigenous name at the center of one of the world's most familiar cityscapes. Later printed spellings and translations are partial evidence rather than final meanings. The name continues to point toward Lenape presence, language, and relationships with this island.
history_content: The name Manhattan comes from the Munsee language of the Lenape people. Early written forms include Manna-hata in 1609. Those spellings preserve clues rather than certainty and belong within Lenape/Munsee language history, not under a single generic Algonquian label.
translation_content:
Manhattan is best introduced as a Native place name with Munsee/Lenape language context. Early written forms include Manna-hata, Mannahattanink, and Monahtanuk. William Wallace Tooker and later writers connected the name with island and hill meanings, but the exact original meaning remains debated because the surviving spellings come through colonial writing.

Why Place Names Matter

“The vitality of a name is lost when the meaning is no longer generally understood.”

— Isaac Taylor, Names and Their Histories (1896), Internet Archive scan leaf 16
whereintheworld_content: Manhattan refers broadly to the modern island. Available evidence does not identify a single village location, earliest written occurrence, or historic boundary.
